# AAPL — Quantitative Fundamental Report | Decision Date 2026-06-22

## 1. Revenue, Earnings, Margin & Cash-Flow Trajectory

Apple's latest reported quarter (Q2 FY-suffix, period end 2026-03-28) delivered revenue of $111.18B, net income of $29.58B, and diluted EPS of $2.01. The QoQ decline (revenue −22.7%, EPS −29.2%) is a normal holiday-to-spring seasonal step-down from the $143.76B / $2.84 EPS Q1 period (2025-12-27). The YoY comparison is far more instructive: revenue +16.6%, EPS +21.8%, and net income +19.4% versus the year-ago Q2 ($95.36B / $1.65 EPS). This confirms the business is not merely sustaining — it is accelerating relative to its own prior-year run rate.

Margin expansion is broad-based. Gross profit rose +22.1% YoY to $54.78B (gross margin ~49.3%), while operating income of $35.88B implies an operating margin of ~32.3% versus ~31.0% a year earlier. Net margin as captured in the trailing ratio panel has widened from 0.243 (June–January 2025 period) to 0.272 (latest). This is a meaningful improvement in profitability quality — revenue is being converted into bottom-line dollars at a higher rate.

Cash generation remains robust. Q2 operating cash flow of $28.70B grew +19.8% YoY (vs. $23.95B in Q2 FY-25). The prior Q1 OCF of $53.92B reflects the usual holiday cash conversion surge. Free cash flow is not available, but operating cash flow figures alone demonstrate Apple continues to convert a large fraction of earnings into cash. No TTM cash flow figure can be cited due to the fiscal-quarter gap in the data.

## 2. Earnings Quality & Balance-Sheet Resilience

Earnings quality indicators are strong. Net income ($29.58B) is fully supported by OCF ($28.70B) in the latest quarter — a near 1:1 conversion ratio that rules out significant accrual divergence. The YoY growth rates for revenue, earnings, and cash flow are tightly clustered (16.6%–21.8%), which signals genuine operating leverage rather than one-time tailwinds inflating headline numbers.

The balance sheet tells an equally constructive story. Total equity has expanded dramatically: $66.76B (2024-12-28) → $66.80B → $65.83B → $88.19B → $106.49B (2026-03-28). Over the same span, total debt has declined from $94.80B to $82.70B. The debt-to-equity ratio has improved from ~1.42 (late 2024) to 0.777 (latest), a structural de-risking of the capital structure. Equity increasing by ~$40B while debt falls by ~$12B reflects aggressive retained-earnings accumulation and/or buyback discipline — Apple is building a thicker equity cushion.

A key caution: the TTM panel is incomplete and cannot be used. The quarterly sequence (Q2→Q1→Q3→Q2) contains a fiscal-gap artifact, and no four-contiguous-quarter trailing sum is valid. All growth conclusions rest on YoY and QoQ comparisons only.

## 3. Valuation vs. Own History (Ratios)

At the latest observation (2026-06-18), AAPL trades at P/E diluted = 35.8x, P/B = 41.2x, P/S = 9.7x, and earnings yield = 2.8%. The 365-day P/E range is 30.5x–43.1x; the current level sits modestly below the midpoint. What is notable is the trajectory: P/E expanded from 31.2x (June 2025) to a peak of 43.1x (December 2025), then steadily contracted to the low-to-mid 30s even as quarterly earnings were improving. The market has been de-rating, not because earnings deteriorated, but because the premium it was willing to pay for those earnings compressed. P/B has fallen even more sharply, from 65.0x peak to 41.2x, partly reflecting the surge in book value described above.

Earnings yield of 2.8% remains well below the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.46%, meaning Apple trades at a negative equity risk premium on a yield basis. For the valuation to be justified purely on income grounds, the market must be pricing in durable mid-to-high-teens earnings growth or significant buyback yield. The margin expansion and YoY growth trends support the former argument, but the absolute multiple does not offer a margin of safety on static fundamentals.

## 4. Price Context vs. Fundamental Path

AAPL closed at $298.01 on 2026-06-18. The 365-day range is $198.96–$317.40; the stock sits ~6% below its high and ~50% above its low. The most recent quarterly move is +19.7% (from $248.96 on 2026-03-19), partially reversing a −9.3% prior-quarter decline. The price has tracked the fundamental inflection — strong Q2 YoY earnings appear to have driven the recovery from the March low. However, the stock has not yet re-tested its $317 high despite earnings growth, consistent with the multiple compression noted above. Price is serving as a secondary confirmation of fundamental improvement, not as the thesis driver.

## 5. Macro & Sentiment Overlays

Macro is mixed but not disqualifying. The Fed funds rate is stable at 3.63% with only marginal easing. The 10-year yield at 4.46% is modestly elevated, pressuring long-duration equities. The yield curve has flattened notably — the 10Y-2Y spread collapsed from 0.49% (late March) to 0.27%, and the 10Y-3M from 0.65% to 0.63% — signaling rising recession risk that could weigh on consumer demand for premium devices. VIX has fallen sharply from ~27 to 16.8, indicating a calmer risk regime. Oil prices have dropped ~14% from peak to $80.35/bbl, easing consumer cost pressures and potentially supporting discretionary spending — a modest tailwind for Apple's hardware cycle.

News sentiment is mildly positive (90-day mean = 0.269 on a [−1, 1] scale) with no discernible deterioration in recent weeks. Sentiment recovered from a brief dip around 2026-06-09 to 2026-06-16. This is a background positive but is the weakest input and does not substitute for the fundamental picture.

## 6. Strongest Quantitative Upside & Downside

**Upside drivers:**
- YoY revenue growth of +16.6% and EPS growth of +21.8% demonstrate real operating momentum; if sustained, the current P/E compresses further without price appreciation.
- Net margin expansion from 0.243 to 0.272 (~290 bps) is structural, not seasonal, and has room to continue if the revenue mix shifts toward higher-margin services.
- Balance sheet leverage has halved (D/E from ~1.42 to 0.78), providing financial flexibility and supporting capital return.
- P/E has compressed from 43.1x to 35.8x while earnings improved — any re-rating toward the midpoint (~38x) at current EPS would imply ~6% upside on the multiple alone.

**Downside risks:**
- The negative equity-risk premium (earnings yield 2.8% vs. 10Y at 4.46%) leaves the stock vulnerable if yields rise further or growth disappoints.
- Flattening yield curve (10Y-2Y at 0.27%) historically precedes economic softening; a downturn in consumer hardware demand would disproportionately impact Apple's revenue base.
- QoQ revenue decline of −22.7% highlights the extreme Q1-dependence; any disruption to the holiday cycle would be amplified.
- The TTM gap makes it impossible to validate trailing twelve-month trends — a material information blind spot.

## 7. Provisional Conclusion

Apple presents a fundamentally attractive profile at the numbers level. YoY growth is in the high-teens to low-20s, margins are expanding, cash conversion is strong, and the balance sheet is rapidly de-risking. The market has partially rewarded this through a +19.7% quarterly price move, but the simultaneous P/E compression from 43x to 36x means the stock is cheaper on an earnings-power basis than it was six months ago — despite better fundamentals. The negative equity-risk premium and flattening yield curve are legitimate macro headwinds that cap the attractiveness at current levels; this is not a "cheap" stock in an absolute sense. However, the trajectory of the business — revenue acceleration, margin expansion, balance sheet improvement, and cash generation — is the most positive quantitative signal in the pack. **The fundamental direction is constructive, but the valuation demands continued high-teens earnings growth to justify the multiple, and the macro backdrop introduces meaningful downside risk.**

# AAPL — Qualitative Assessment (2026-06-22)

## 1. Business / Franchise Read

Apple's franchise quality remains best-in-class by nearly every structural measure. The company posted record results in both fiscal quarters reported to date: Q1 FY2026 delivered $143.8B in revenue (up 16% YoY) with $42.1B net income, while Q2 FY2026 set a March-quarter record at $111.2B revenue (up 17%) and $29.6B net income. Services revenue hit an all-time high of $31B in Q2, operating at approximately 76% gross margins, and has become the primary driver of overall margin expansion — Q2 gross margin reached 49%, a multi-year peak. Operating cash flow totaled $82.6B in the first half of FY2026 alone.

The ecosystem remains Apple's core competitive moat. Over 2.5 billion active devices are installed globally, iPhone retention sits around 90%, and the company holds the world's most valuable brand at $608B (Brand Finance). Market share data shows gains across segments: iPhone volume share rose from 19% to 21% YoY, iPad from 34% to 37%, and Apple Watch from 20% to 23% (Counterpoint, Q1 2025 vs Q1 2026). Revenue share gains are even larger — iPhone revenue share jumped from 43% to 48%, iPad from 54% to 60% — reflecting Apple's premium ASP strategy compounding on unit gains. Greater China revenue grew 38% YoY in Q1 FY2026, defying years of bearish predictions.

Capital allocation remains shareholder-friendly: a new $100B buyback authorization was announced alongside Q2 results, the quarterly dividend was raised 4% to $0.27, and $36B in stock was repurchased in the first half alone. Management's stated goal of moving toward net-cash-neutral over time implies continued heavy returns.

The strategic question is AI positioning. Apple's approach is notably capital-light relative to peers — Q2 capex was modest compared to hyperscalers deploying hundreds of billions. Instead, Apple licensed Google's Gemini models to power a rebuilt Siri and "Apple Intelligence" features, announced at WWDC 2026 (June 8). This partnership is pragmatic — Apple pays roughly $1B annually — but creates a structural dependency on a rival's technology and highlights that Apple has fallen behind on foundational AI models. The flip side is Apple's unique distribution advantage: any capable AI model, once integrated, is instantly delivered to two billion devices through software updates, giving Apple enormous monetization leverage regardless of which model powers the back end.

## 2. Recent Developments (Dated Events)

**WWDC / Siri AI Reaction (June 8–18):** Apple unveiled AI-powered Siri at WWDC on June 8, featuring multi-step requests, on-device context awareness, and cross-device functionality. The stock dropped ~3.6% on the announcement as investors viewed the rollout as incremental — English-only in the US initially, with a beta launch later in 2026 and limited third-party app access. By June 18, Wall Street had warmed: shares recovered, with Maxim Group reiterating a Buy with a $350 target, and analysts citing Apple's monetization strategy through premium service tiers and a capital-light AI approach.

**Intel Chip Partnership (June 18):** President Trump announced that Apple has agreed to work with Intel to design and build chips in the United States. Intel shares surged ~11% on the news. However, neither Apple nor Intel has issued formal confirmation of terms or scope. This remains unconfirmed as of the decision date. If real, it would represent meaningful supply chain diversification away from TSMC.

**Memory Cost Pressure (June 17–19):** CEO Tim Cook warned that memory chip prices have "quadrupled" due to AI data center demand, calling it a "100-year flood." Cook indicated Apple will raise prices across its product lineup to offset costs, with one source citing potential ~$200 iPhone price increases. This is a real margin headwind, though Apple's brand strength and ecosystem lock-in provide meaningful pricing power.

**Regulatory / Supply Chain Risks (June 12–16):** Italy's antitrust regulator opened an investigation into Apple's iCloud terms. Separately, a Tata Electronics plant in India (iPhone component supplier) faces environmental compliance allegations regarding groundwater contamination, introducing operational risk in Apple's China-diversification strategy. These are incremental risk factors rather than existential threats at this stage.

## 3. Material Risks and Offsets

**AI execution risk:** Apple's Siri AI is powered by Google Gemini, not proprietary models. A botched rollout or continued dependence on a competitor's technology could confirm Apple lost a structural step in AI. *Offset:* Apple's distribution scale and on-device processing provide a unique monetization platform regardless of model supplier; the measured capex approach preserves cash flow relative to peers burning hundreds of billions on AI infrastructure.

**iPhone concentration (~59% of revenue):** A weak product cycle or supply disruption could disproportionately impact results. *Offset:* Services revenue (now $31B quarterly at 76% margins) and the installed base of 2.5B devices increasingly cushion hardware cyclicality.

**Regulatory / antitrust:** DOJ lawsuit, EU Digital Markets Act, and Italy iCloud probe could force changes to the App Store commission model — Apple's highest-margin business. *Offset:* No definitive ruling as of the decision date; bulls argue services growth can continue even with structural changes.

**Memory / component cost inflation:** Dramatic DRAM/NAND price increases threaten margins. *Offset:* Pricing power from brand strength and ecosystem lock-in; Cook has signaled willingness to raise prices.

**Supply chain concentration and diversification execution:** China remains a manufacturing dependency; India diversification faces fresh compliance headwinds at Tata Electronics. The unconfirmed Intel foundry deal, if real, would help long-term but carries its own execution risk.

**Leveraged capital structure:** D/E ratio of 2.61 and current ratio of 0.86 reflect aggressive buyback activity funded partly by debt. *Offset:* $82.6B in operating cash flow in H1 FY2026 more than covers obligations; this is a deliberate capital allocation choice, not financial distress.

## 4. Qualitative Assessment

**Positive.** Apple's franchise quality — ecosystem stickiness, Services margin expansion to 49% overall gross margin, record cash generation, and accelerating share gains across every hardware segment — is among the strongest in global equities. The capital-light AI strategy, while initially disappointing to the market, is proving defensible as peers' AI capex faces scrutiny. Pricing power offsets component inflation. The financial trajectory is firmly positive: record revenues, record margins, record cash flows, and aggressive shareholder returns. Recent developments (WWDC recovery, confirmed memory pricing power, unconfirmed but strategically significant Intel deal) lean supportive. The principal risk is execution on AI integration into the ecosystem at scale; a failed Siri rollout would reinforce the narrative that Apple's AI deficit is structural rather than timing-related. On balance, the structural franchise read supports fundamental attractiveness despite elevated valuations and regulatory overhang.

views.rationale: Apple presents a fundamentally strong profile with accelerating YoY growth (revenue +16.6%, EPS +21.8% in Q2 FY2026), broad-based margin expansion (net margin from 0.243 to 0.272, gross margin at 49.3%), robust cash generation ($28.7B OCF in Q2, $82.6B H1), and a rapidly improving balance sheet (D/E from ~1.42 to 0.78). The franchise is best-in-class: 2.5B active devices, ~90% iPhone retention, and market share gains across all hardware segments (iPhone volume 19%→21%, revenue share 43%→48%). Valuation is the key constraint: P/E of 35.8x has compressed from 43.1x peak but still demands sustained high-teens growth, and the earnings yield of 2.8% sits well below the 10Y Treasury at 4.46%, implying a negative equity risk premium. The stock is cheaper on an earnings-power basis than six months ago despite better fundamentals — a constructive setup. Near-term catalysts are modest: WWDC AI reaction has stabilized (stock recovered from initial selloff), the $100B buyback authorization provides support, and Tim Cook's pricing-power signal on memory costs is a credible margin defense. However, the flattening yield curve (10Y-2Y at 0.27%) signals recession risk that could pressure consumer hardware demand, and the negative ERP leaves little margin of safety. The score reflects strong fundamentals and trajectory (pillar 1) partially offset by a still-elevated absolute multiple (pillar 2), with a modest positive bump from the WWDC stabilization and buyback catalyst (pillar 3).
